parametric-derivatives-s1.title: A path with direction arrows and two marked times
parametric-derivatives-s1.text: A point moves along the path $x(t) = t^3 - 3t$, $y(t) = 4 - t^2$ for $-2 \le t \le 2$. The graph shows the path; the arrows give the direction of increasing $t$, and the points where $t = -1$ and $t = 2$ are marked.

parametric-derivatives-s2.title: A curve known only from a table
parametric-derivatives-s2.text: A curve is traced by $(x(t), y(t))$, where $x$ and $y$ are differentiable functions of $t$. The table gives selected values.

table.caption: Values of $x$, $y$ and their derivatives with respect to $t$

mistakes.why: That is $\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$, upside down. The slope is $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$: the vertical rate over the horizontal rate.
That is $\frac{dy}{dt}$ alone, how fast $y$ changes per unit of time. Divide by $\frac{dx}{dt} = 9$ to get the change in $y$ per unit of $x$.

items.q: Write an equation of the line tangent to the path at the point where $t = 2$.

mistakes.why: The slope is $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{-4}{9}$; this line uses the reciprocal.
$-4$ is $\frac{dy}{dt}$, a rate per unit of time. The slope of the line is $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = -\frac{4}{9}$.
The point is $(x(2), y(2)) = (2, 0)$, so the line is $y - 0 = -\frac{4}{9}(x - 2)$: subtract 2.

items.q: Which statement describes the tangent line at the point where $t = -1$?
options: It is vertical, because $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} \ne 0$ there
It does not exist, because $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is undefined there

why.correct: At $t = -1$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = 3(1) - 3 = 0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2 \ne 0$. The point moves straight up for an instant, so the tangent line is vertical: the path turns from moving right to moving left at $(2, 3)$.
options: $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ makes the horizontal motion stop, which gives a vertical tangent. A horizontal tangent needs $\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$.
$\frac{dy}{dt} = 2$ is a rate per unit of time, not the slope; the slope divides by $\frac{dx}{dt}$, which is 0 here.
Right: no horizontal motion and nonzero vertical motion give a vertical tangent line.
An undefined slope is the slope of a vertical line; the tangent line exists and is vertical.

items.q: For which values of $t$ is the point moving to the left and up at the same time?

why.correct: Left means $\frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 3 < 0$, so $-1 < t < 1$. Up means $\frac{dy}{dt} = -2t > 0$, so $t < 0$. Both hold for $-1 < t < 0$, the part of the path from $(2, 3)$ to the top, $(0, 4)$.
options: Here $\frac{dx}{dt} > 0$ (for example $3(1.5)^2 - 3 > 0$), so the point moves right and up.
Here $\frac{dy}{dt} = -2t < 0$, so the point moves left and down.

items.q: At which point is the tangent line to the path horizontal?

why.correct: Horizontal tangent: $\frac{dy}{dt} = -2t = 0$ with $\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0$. That is $t = 0$, where $\frac{dx}{dt} = -3$, at the point $(0, 4)$.
options: There $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} \ne 0$: those tangents are vertical.
The crossing point has two tangent lines, one for each pass, and neither is horizontal.
$y = 0$ is where the path meets the $x$-axis; the slope there is $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \pm\frac{4}{9}$, not 0.

items.q: Find the slope of the curve at the point where $t = 3$.

mistakes.why: That divides $x'(3)$ by $y'(3)$. The slope is $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{y'(3)}{x'(3)}$.
That is $y'(3)$ alone, a rate per unit of $t$. Divide it by $x'(3) = -4$.
That divides the values $y(3)$ and $x(3)$; the slope uses the derivatives $y'(3)$ and $x'(3)$.

items.q: Write an equation of the line tangent to the curve at the point where $t = 0$.

mistakes.why: The slope is $\frac{y'(0)}{x'(0)} = \frac{-2}{3}$; this line uses $\frac{x'(0)}{y'(0)}$.
The point is $(x(0), y(0)) = (1, 4)$. The time $t = 0$ is not the $x$-coordinate; use $x - 1$.
The coordinates are swapped: the point is $(1, 4)$, with $x = 1$ and $y = 4$.

why.correct: At $t = 0$ the point is $(x(0), y(0)) = (1, 4)$ and the slope is $\frac{y'(0)}{x'(0)} = -\frac{2}{3}$, so $y = 4 - \frac{2}{3}(x - 1)$.

items.q: What does the table tell you about the tangent lines at $t = 1$ and at $t = 2$?

why.correct: At $t = 1$: $y'(1) = 0$ and $x'(1) = 1 \ne 0$, so the slope is 0 (horizontal). At $t = 2$: $x'(2) = 0$ and $y'(2) = 2 \ne 0$, so the tangent is vertical.
options: Right: a zero numerator ($y'$) gives a horizontal tangent; a zero denominator ($x'$) with a nonzero $y'$ gives a vertical one.
This swaps the two cases. $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y'}{x'}$ is 0 when $y' = 0$: horizontal.
At $t = 2$ it is $x'$ that is 0, not $y'$: that tangent is vertical.
These divide the coordinates $y(t)$ by $x(t)$; slopes come from the derivatives.

items.q: In which direction is the point moving at $t = 3$?

why.correct: $x'(3) = -4 < 0$, so $x$ is decreasing: the point moves left. $y'(3) = 3 > 0$, so $y$ is increasing: it moves up.
options: $x'(3) = -4$ is negative, so $x$ is decreasing: left, not right.
$y'(3) = 3$ is positive, so the point moves up.
Both signs are reversed here: $x'(3) < 0$ and $y'(3) > 0$.

items.q: A curve is given by $x = e^t$, $y = t^2 + 1$. Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $t = 1$.

mistakes.why: That is $\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$. Put the rate of $y$ on top: $\frac{2t}{e^t}$.
That is $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2t$ alone. Divide by $\frac{dx}{dt} = e^t$, which is $e$ at $t = 1$.

why.correct: $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2t$ and $\frac{dx}{dt} = e^t$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2t}{e^t}$, which is $\frac{2}{e}$ at $t = 1$.

items.q: A curve is given by $x = 3\cos t$, $y = 2\sin t$. Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of $t$.

mistakes.why: That is $\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$. The slope is $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{2\cos t}{-3\sin t}$.
The derivative of $\cos t$ is $-\sin t$, so $\frac{dx}{dt} = -3\sin t$ and the slope is negative where $\sin t$ and $\cos t$ are both positive.

why.correct: $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2\cos t$ and $\frac{dx}{dt} = -3\sin t$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2\cos t}{-3\sin t} = -\frac{2\cos t}{3\sin t}$ wherever $\sin t \ne 0$.

items.q: A curve is given by $x = t^2 + 1$, $y = t^3 - 12t$. At which points is the tangent line horizontal?

options: At $t = 0$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} = -12 \ne 0$: that tangent is vertical.
These write $(t, y)$; the $x$-coordinate is $x(\pm 2) = 5$, not $t$.

items.q: A curve is given by $x = t^2 + 1$, $y = t\sin t$ for $0 < t < 3$. Find the value of $t$ at which the tangent line is horizontal.

mistakes.why: That solves $t\cos t = 0$, the product rule with the $\sin t$ term dropped. $\frac{dy}{dt} = \sin t + t\cos t$.

why.correct: Horizontal tangent: $\frac{dy}{dt} = \sin t + t\cos t = 0$ with $\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t \ne 0$. Solving on the calculator (radian mode) gives $t \approx 2.029$ (2.028 also earns the point); there $\frac{dx}{dt} \approx 4.06 \ne 0$.

items.q: A curve is given by $x = x(t)$, $y = y(t)$. Which expression gives the slope of the tangent line at a point where $\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0$?

why.correct: By the chain rule $\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$: rise per unit of time over run per unit of time.
options: This is the reciprocal of the slope, run over rise.
This is how fast $y$ changes per unit of time, not per unit of $x$.
Multiplying the rates has no meaning here; the chain rule gives a quotient.
Right: the chain rule, solved for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.

items.q: The curve $x = t^2$, $y = t^3 - 3t$ passes through $(3, 0)$ twice, at $t = -\sqrt{3}$ and at $t = \sqrt{3}$. What can be said about the slope of the curve at $(3, 0)$?
options: There are two tangent lines, with slopes $-\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{3}$
There is one slope, found by putting $x = 3$ into a formula for $\frac{dy}{dx}$
It does not exist, because the curve crosses itself there

why.correct: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t}$. At $t = \sqrt{3}$: $\frac{6}{2\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}$. At $t = -\sqrt{3}$: $-\sqrt{3}$. Each pass through the point has its own tangent line, which is why slopes are found from $t$, not from the point.
options: The height of a point says nothing about its slope; compute $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$ at each $t$.
Right: one tangent line for each time the curve passes through the point.
$\frac{dy}{dx}$ here is a formula in $t$, and two values of $t$ give $x = 3$, with different slopes.
Each pass has a well-defined tangent line; there are simply two of them.

items.q: A point moves along a curve. At time $t = 2$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = 4$ and the slope of the curve is $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{2}$. Find $\frac{dy}{dt}$ at $t = 2$.

mistakes.why: That divides $\frac{dx}{dt}$ by $\frac{dy}{dx}$. The chain rule multiplies: $\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$.
That divides the slope by $\frac{dx}{dt}$. Multiply instead: $-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4$.

why.correct: $\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt} = -\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 = -2$: $y$ is decreasing at 2 units per unit of time.
